19687.etyen:
Compound of Giss (“G-sharp”) + dur (“major”), literally “G-sharp major”.
The first element Giss (“G-sharp”) consists of G (“G”) and -iss (“sharp”), the latter from German German -is (“sharp”); compare German Gis (“G-sharp”). The second element dur (“major”) is through German German Dur (“major”) from Latin Latin dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Italic Proto-Italic *dūros (“hard”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós (“long, distant”), from the root *dweh₂- (“long, distant; to remove, separate”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk Giss-dur, Swedish Giss-du

487.etyen:
Borrowed from Italian a conto (“on account”), with the spelling of Italian conto (“account, bill”) adapted to Norwegian konto (“account”).
The Italian expression consists of a (“to, at, on”) and conto (“account, bill”), literally “on account”.
The first element, a (“to, at, on”), is inherited from Latin ad (“to, towards, at”), from Proto-Italic *ad (“to, towards”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”).
The second element, conto (“account, bill”), is from Vulgar Latin *contus (“calculation, account”) or *comptus, from Latin computus (“calculation, account”), from computō (“to calculate, re

1000167.etyen:
Borrowed from Latin Christianus (“Christian; follower of Christ”), from Ancient Greek Χριστιανός (Khristianós, “Christian; follower of Christ”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós, “Christ; the anointed one”). The word was originally an appellation for followers of Christ before becoming a personal name. First attested in the 14th century in Norway.
Compare Danish Christian, Swedish Christian, German Christian and English Christian.

en.g: Fredrikstad (the administrative center, municipality, and city in Viken, Eastern Norway, Norway)

1000679.etyen:
Fredrik + stad, first part named after Frederick II of Denmark, the King of Denmark and Norway and Duke of Schleswig and Holstein from 1559 until his death in 1588, the city was the first in Norway to be named after a person.
Prior to 1877, the name was spelled Frederiksstad, then from 1877–1888 it was written as Fredriksstad, and finally since 1889 it has been spelled in its current form: Fredrikstad.

1000935.etyen: Learned borrowing from Old Norse Rogaland, from the genitive plural of rygir (“the people living in Rogaland”) + land (“land, region”). The first element roga- is an older form than rygja-, as in Ryfylke. The county was formerly called Stavanger amt, but the name Rogaland was taken into use as the county name in 1919.

1001959.etyen:
Borrowed from Latin būglōssa (“oxtongue, bugloss”), from Ancient Greek βούγλωσσον (boúglōsson, “ox tongue; bugloss”), itself from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). Literally “ox tongue”; the plant name refers to the shape and roughness of its leaves.
Compare Catalan buglossa, French buglosse, English bugloss, and Portuguese buglossa (“bugloss”).

en.g: Lærdalen; a valley in Lærdal municipality, Vestland, Norway, a valley in Lærdal municipality extending inland from the head of Lærdalsfjorden, through which Lærdalselva flows
x: Tidlig den næste Morgen (Onsdag) var jeg atter paa Skierne, og nu gik det paa et maadeligt Føre opigjennem Lærdalen.
Early the next morning (Wednesday) I was back on my skis, and now I proceeded on rather mediocre snow conditions up through Lærdalen.

1005031.etyen:
From Lærdal (“place name”) + -en (“definite singular suffix”), literally “the Lærdal”.
The base name Lærdal continues Middle Norwegian Lærdall, from Old Norse Læradalr, probably reduced from earlier *Lærardalr. The first element is the genitive of a lost river name *Lærr, while the second is dalr (“valley, dale”). The origin of the river name is uncertain.
